tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Main findings page › 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure, 3rd bullet
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review's systematic review found six studies of second-hand exposure to vaping aerosol using a variety of biomarkers, none from the UK, with exposure varying greatly from people at home to people at an indoor vaping convention. Short exposures did not produce detectable changes in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines; longer exposures during heavy sustained vaping were associated with significant increases in nicotine or in metabolites of potential toxicants. The main findings page states no significant increase in toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape.

tasks.locator: Summary page › Chapter 10: Respiratory diseases › Main findings › Respiratory tests and imaging, last paragraph; Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Secondhand exposure, 1st paragraph; Comparisons with other reports, 6th paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review concluded there was insufficient evidence on whether acute second-hand vaping affects lung function; only 2 small studies at serious risk of bias included second-hand exposure for heart rate or blood pressure, so no conclusion could be drawn. It repeats the Committee on Toxicity's conclusion that vaping is associated with some emissions of nicotine into ambient air, so that pharmacological effects of nicotine in ambient air may occur in some individuals, and says its own two small studies of short-term second-hand exposure did not allow clear conclusions.

tasks.locator: Chapter 16 › Overall findings in the context of our series of evidence reviews, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The UK review's authors recall that their 2015 report estimated vaping to be at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful to the person), a statement offered to help the public and professionals grasp the size of the gap. They write that summarising relative risks across many products, behaviours and biomarkers can be simplistic and misread; that, on the evidence reviewed, they judge the at-least-95% estimate still broadly accurate for the short and medium term; that it may now be more fitting to summarise their findings with their other firm statement, that vaping carries only a small share of smoking's risks; and that this does not mean vaping is free of risk, particularly for people who have never smoked. They add that the size of this gap is not reflected in current public perceptions. The pages read give no source or calculation for the 2015 figure. This is the authors' judgment on an estimate from their own earlier report.
tasks.quote: vaping poses only a small fraction of the risks of smoking

tasks.locator: Main findings page › 2.1 Overall conclusions; 2.2 Biomarkers of toxicant exposure; 2.3 Biomarkers of potential harm
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's overall conclusions, on the evidence it reviewed: in the short and medium term vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks; it is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked; evidence is mostly limited to short and medium term effects, so studies of vaping for more than 12 months are needed; more standardised methods in future studies would improve interpretation. Biomarkers of toxicant exposure: significantly lower exposure to harmful substances from vaping than from smoking, as shown by biomarkers associated with the risk of cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions; similar or higher exposure than with not using nicotine products; no significant increase of toxicant biomarkers after short-term second-hand exposure among people who do not smoke or vape. Biomarkers of potential harm: the team could draw only limited conclusions, but better-run studies of short and medium term risks found no major causes of concern associated with vaping.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Main findings › Nicotine; Volatile organic compounds; Tobacco specific nitrosamines; Other potential toxicants; Carbon monoxide; Metals
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The systematic review's biomarker chapter (60 studies of nicotine, 24 of volatile organic compounds, 28 of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, 9 of other toxicants, 33 of carbon monoxide and 10 of metals; designs, definitions and exposure periods varied and few studies were from the UK). People who vape compared with people who smoke, pooled analyses: nicotine and its breakdown products not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; volatile organic compound breakdown products mostly significantly lower in 15 analyses (acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, 1,3-butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower), with formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; nitrosamine breakdown products significantly lower in all 5 analyses (NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower in both analyses; metals mixed. People who vape compared with people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher, as expected (4 analyses); volatile organic compounds not significantly different in the pooled analyses except the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses, which cannot separate vaping from earlier tobacco use, while a randomised trial and a cross-over study suggest levels might fall to those of people who use no nicotine; metals mostly higher; carbon monoxide similar to non-use in interventional studies of people who switched completely.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Evidence reviewed, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Implications › Vaping reduces toxicant exposure compared with cigarette smoking; Methodological improvements needed; Improvements in definitions needed, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review states that studies used a range of definitions, with some classing people who vape and smoke, vape occasionally or vape daily as one group; that studies with more than one time point mostly explored acute exposure (single use to 7 days) or followed people for 8 days to 12 months, so findings on vaping for more than 12 months could not be summarised; and that few studies could be pooled. Its implications: compared with smoking, vaping leads to a substantial reduction in biomarkers of toxicant exposure associated with cigarette smoking, but the degree of any residual risk remains unclear, mainly because comparisons are lacking between people who smoked for many years and have quit and now vape and those who have quit and do not vape, and with people who have never smoked or vaped; past tobacco use can greatly affect many of the biomarkers and most people who vape smoked for many years before; and no difference between people who vape and people who use no nicotine could reflect insensitive measures, background exposure, or truly similar exposure.

tasks.locator: Chapter 7: Biomarkers of exposure › Implications › More research needed on biomarkers of exposure among vapers, 2nd paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review states that in its meta-analyses many findings were from tobacco industry-funded randomised trials conducted in confinement (closed settings such as research centres or hospitals) for periods of up to 7 days, and that future research needs to include more independent research on biomarkers of exposure in people who vape, people who smoke and people who use no tobacco or nicotine, outside confinement and with longer follow-up. The pages read do not say how many pooled results these trials make up or whether their results differ from the independent studies.

tasks.locator: Chapter 8: Biomarkers of potential harm › Main findings › Inflammation; Endothelial function, last paragraph; Implications › Need to distinguish biomarkers of potential harm from smoking or vaping from other sources, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review covered 41 studies (43 publications) of oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function and platelet activation; most assessed acute vaping effects and most had methodological concerns. Inflammation: pooled cross-sectional studies showed lower blood C-reactive protein and sICAM-1 in people who vape than in people who smoke, but controlled and longitudinal studies did not confirm this. Endothelial function: acute sessions of vaping (with and without nicotine) and of smoking produced similar short-term reductions in flow-mediated dilation, while a single randomised trial found that switching from smoking to vaping for 4 weeks significantly improved it; the review writes that acute vaping might cause endothelial dysfunction as much as acute smoking, and that switching might improve endothelial function in the longer term. It concludes that most studies in the chapter cannot inform medium or long term risks through these biomarkers, and that studies are needed with people who use no nicotine as a comparison group and longer follow-up.

tasks.locator: Chapter 9: Cancers › Main findings › Toxicants and carcinogens; Cancer risks; Inflammation and oxidative stress; Cell and animal studies; Implications › Longer follow up periods are needed
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's cancer chapter calls the exposure-biomarker studies conclusive evidence that vaping generally leads to lower exposure to many of the carcinogens responsible for the health risks of smoking (exposure, not cancer). It adds that the National Academies found no available evidence on whether the chemicals in vaping aerosols or vaping behaviour were associated with cancer risk relative to smoking or non-use; that evidence on inflammation and oxidative stress is insufficient for conclusions; that no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; and that cell and animal studies suggest vaping aerosols are not benign for people who have never smoked while also suggesting alterations in gene expression to a lower extent than tobacco smoke, though translating such studies to human risk is challenging. Its implications: studies of exposure biomarkers need longer follow-up to tell whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking.

tasks.locator: Chapter 11: Cardiovascular diseases › Main findings › Heart rate; Blood pressure; Peripheral resistance and arterial stiffness; Comparisons with other reports, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Implications, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review concludes that the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, but that based on the toxicant profile in vaping products and aerosols the risk is expected to be much less than that of cigarette smoking (an expectation, not a measured rate). It states that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis; that 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute exposure studies, which cannot answer questions about the cardiovascular health outcomes most relevant to public health; and that studies comparing rates of cardiovascular disease between people who use no nicotine, tobacco, or vaping products are needed. Measured: immediately after use vaping increased heart rate less than smoking; in pooled cross-sectional studies of longer vaping (at least 3 months or one year) people who vaped had lower blood pressure than people who smoked and no difference from people who neither vaped nor smoked; the longest follow-up of arterial stiffness after switching was 4 months.

tasks.locator: Chapter 16 › introductory paragraphs, 2nd paragraph; Evidence statements, 1st paragraph; Chapter 1 › Issues addressed, 3rd paragraph and its list; Authors and citation
tasks.source_read: GOV.UK HTML: summary page and main findings page of the 2022 evidence update (the PDF was not opened)
tasks.extracted: The review's closing chapter states that, despite the increase in research on vaping since 2015, weaknesses in the choice of assessments and biomarkers, populations, groups studied and exposure, and study designs all limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Its 61 evidence statements broadly follow the National Academies' definitions of level of evidence, and the authors write that, as the National Academies noted, the framework is a guide and a great deal of expert judgement, here by the report's co-authors, is involved. The scope left out two questions: vaping and later smoking (a Cochrane review of people under 30 was examining it) and the effectiveness of vaping for stopping smoking (covered in the series' previous report and by a Cochrane living review). The report is the eighth in a series described as independent and commissioned by Public Health England and then the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; it was led by academics at King's College London with international collaborators (eight authors are named); the pages read carry no competing-interest statement.

tasks.locator: Abstract › Data sources, Data synthesis; Methods › 1st paragraph; Inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The Australian review combines an umbrella review of 8 major independent reviews published 2017 to 2021 with a top-up systematic review (searched July 2020, for studies published July 2017 to July 2020), 400 publications in all, registered in advance; the top-up studies were appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the evidence graded with GRADE and the National Academies framework. It is based on work commissioned by the Australian Department of Health. It looked at the health effects of e-cigarettes in people and excluded animal, in vitro and biomarker studies as outside its scope, so the biomarker evidence on which the UK review's conclusion on relative harm mainly rests was not counted.
